newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish PM welcomes NATO "super PfP" - paper.
newsitem.headline: Finnish PM welcomes NATO "super PfP" - paper.

text.p: Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen welcomes efforts by NATO to develop an expanded Partnership for Peace to embrace non-aligned states and those left out of an expanded alliance, a newspaper said on Friday.

In an interview with leading daily Helsingin Sanomat, Lipponen was asked if Finland, which shares an 800 mile (1,300 km) border with Russia, was ready for the western alliance's offer of an expanded Partnership for Peace (PfP).

"Finland is favourably disposed towards it," he was quoted as saying. "For Finland NATO is above all a partner in maintaining stability in northern Europe. The United States's presence in Europe is necessary."

NATO leaders and diplomats are proposing intensified cooperation in PfP, which was originally aimed at uniting former Cold War foes, to appease former Soviet countries likely to be left out of the first wave of its expansion.

Lipponen said Finland, which joined PfP in 1994, would plan to keep taking part in any continued international peacekeeping efforts in Bosnia, although probably with a smaller or different unit. There are currently about 400 Finnish troops in Bosnia.
Finland joined the European Union in 1995 but is not seeking NATO membership.

Lipponen, who according to the Finnish constitution as prime minister plays a secondary role to the president in foreign policy, said Russia should be integrated and tightly involved in Europe's new security system.
Asked how he felt about changes in the Russian leadership, he said: "Russian citizens have had their say on the continuation of the reform policy, and they also want stable conditions.
"I do not see reason for any serious concern. If the nationalistic tone were to grow harsher, it would be worrisome."
